sections.title: Replacing old metal tiles: tile again or long-run?

blocks.text: Both choices are possible. Riggall Roofing describes converting metal tiles to long-run with new purlins. A new tile system also needs its own compatible support arrangement. The choice should follow roof condition, desired appearance and the complete replacement quote, not a presumption that every old tile roof must stay tiled.

blocks.title: Why removing the covering can reveal another scope of work

blocks.text: The Tamahere example replaced asphalt shingles, not old metal tiles. It is included to illustrate damaged plywood and framing discovered during replacement, not to imply how often tile roofs are affected. Sagging, decay and damaged framing must be assessed and addressed; a different covering is not a structural repair.

blocks.title: What about laying new tiles over an existing roof?

blocks.text: Gerard describes a CF Shake overlay option for certain Decramastic roofs. This is a separate specified system, not an automatic substitute for removal. Have the existing structure, substrate, moisture condition, asbestos risk and warranty eligibility assessed first. An ordinary removal quote and an overlay quote have different scopes.

Older textured metal tiles may contain asbestos in their coating. Do not identify asbestos from appearance alone, scrape a sample yourself or start abrasive cleaning. Arrange competent assessment and appropriate testing before work that could disturb suspect material. Any asbestos work needs a separate scope and price.

Consent is not determined only by calling a job a reroof. MBIE’s repair and replacement exemption has conditions and exclusions. Ask the designer or council to check the actual changes, especially damaged structural work; do not rely on a general contractor cost guide as legal approval.

blocks.title: Working with an older stone-chip roof?
blocks.text: Read the testing and replacement considerations before choosing a removal allowance.
blocks.label: Read the Decramastic answer

sections.title: Maintenance, warranties and coastal conditions

blocks.text: A warranty term is not a measured service life. Obtain the current warranty for the exact finish, environment and installation type, plus the installer’s workmanship terms. Gerard’s current documents separate standard, corrosive-environment and overlay provisions and attach maintenance conditions.

blocks.title: What changes once the roof is in service?

blocks.text: Gerard’s roof-care guide says water blasting is not recommended for removing organic growth from its roof tiles. It calls for appropriate treatment and attention to corrosion; it does not promise a maintenance-free roof. Use a qualified roof-care contractor and the current product instructions. The separate wall-cladding pressure guidance is not a roof-cleaning instruction.

Ask about coastal exposure, compatible flashings, runoff from other metals and any solar or skylight additions before purchase. Where roof water supplies a tank, obtain product and cleaning instructions covering drinking-water collection. Do not assume a roofing appraisal itself assesses potable-water suitability.

Modern stone-coated metal tiles should not be called Decramastic as a catch-all. NZMRM explains the historical change from bituminous to acrylic-based coatings; an old article’s brand list or warranty period is not today’s product specification.

sections.title: How to use this evidence to get a comparable quote

blocks.text: This review separates manufacturer specifications, published guide prices, project accounts and RoofHub calculations. Multiple pages from one manufacturer do not provide independent confirmation. Reading an undated price today does not make it a quotation for today’s roof.

items: Send the same measured roof area and plan/actual basis to each quoting installer.
Name the exact panel profile, finish and colour, not just “metal tile”.
Request panel quantities or a schedule, with the allowance and pack/minimum terms identified.
Confirm underlay, battens or decking, trims, valleys, fixings and installation scope.
For replacement, separate removal, disposal, asbestos assessment and timber repair allowances.
State access/scaffolding, delivery, GST, warranty and quote validity explicitly.

blocks.text: Prices remain in their source’s stated unit and tax basis. Historical guides keep their dates; missing panel rates are not imputed. Where published coverage numbers disagree, this page flags them and disables the affected automatic preset. RoofHub does not sell the listed panels or certify an installation.

blocks.title: Bring the same brief to your roofing quotes
blocks.text: Send RoofHub your question and the roof system you are considering. Include the scope you need checked, not just a target total.
blocks.label: Ask about a pressed-tile roof

faqs.q: Is pressed metal tile still used on new homes?
faqs.a: Yes. The Fowler Huapai and Abron Brookfield showhomes document metal-tile roofs, and Gerard has a dedicated new-build range. These are examples, not a measured national market share.

faqs.q: Is Metrotile a separate current NZ manufacturer comparison?
faqs.a: Gerard’s NZ site says Metrotile is now Gerard. Keep legacy names on historical observations, but do not count both brands as independent current pricing samples.

faqs.q: Can I buy panels at the prices shown above?
faqs.a: No. Those are installed budgeting observations, some historical and one undated. This review has not established a verified current per-panel NZ retail rate; use a written supplier quote for the worksheet.

faqs.q: How many panels cover a 200 m² roof?
faqs.a: At a published density of 2.15 panels/m², 200 m² of actual roof area gives 430 panels before extra allowance and pack rounding. A 2.2-panel profile gives 440. These are planning quantities, not a roof-face cutting schedule.

faqs.q: Do all metal tiles use the same battens?
faqs.a: No. The support system is profile-specific, and some concealed-fix systems involve plywood. Confirm the selected system’s appraisal and installation details before pricing or ordering supports.

faqs.q: Does a stone-chip roof automatically contain asbestos?
faqs.a: No. Age and appearance cannot establish asbestos content. Suspect older material needs competent assessment and appropriate testing before disturbance. Modern product specifications and an old roof’s test result are different kinds of evidence.

faqs.q: Can an old metal-tile roof become a long-run roof?
faqs.a: Yes, subject to the condition and design of the roof. The installer may need to replace or reconfigure supports for the selected long-run system. Structural defects are not solved simply by changing the covering.

faqs.q: Does the worksheet provide a full installed quote?
faqs.a: No. It estimates panel quantities and, only when you enter a price, a panel-only subtotal. The detailed estimator and an installer’s project quote are the next steps for accessories, labour and site work.

tray.title: Tray and standing-seam roofing NZ: what changes the cost?
tray.description: Compare NZ architectural tray systems, pan widths, support requirements, historical installed costs and documented architectural projects.
tray.answer: Tray and standing-seam roofing describe a group of architectural systems, not a single product. The fixing method, seam detail, base metal and support build-up can differ. Price the exact system with its substrate, clips and flashings rather than comparing pan prices alone.

sections.title: Which system differences matter?

blocks.caption: Two different architectural system examples
heads: Why it matters to a quote

cells: 470 mm nominal cover, concealed clips, published 3° starting minimum.
Its support approach can avoid a full substrate where designed to the manufacturer’s requirements.
Choose the actual Eurotray variant and build-up, not the family name alone.

blocks.text: Do not treat “standing seam” as a guarantee that the seams are all formed or installed in the same way. The name on the quote should lead to an exact specification and compatible detail set.

sections.title: Why can substrate change the price?

blocks.text: Support is part of the roof system. A quote that includes plywood and associated preparation is not comparable to a pan-only price. Conversely, applying a blanket plywood allowance to a system designed without it can overstate the cost.

Metalcraft describes Espan’s clip system as fixing to purlins at specified spans. In Dimond’s Eel House case, the curved aluminium Eurotray roofing was installed over plywood. These are distinct documented build-ups, not proof that every tray needs or avoids plywood.

sections.title: What installed pricing has been published?

blocks.text: These are historical guide observations with different scopes and tax information. They are not three independent current quotes for the same tray system. The broad architectural allowance in the detailed estimator remains a planning input, not a manufacturer tariff.

sections.title: What do architectural projects reveal?

blocks.text: Curved geometry, roof-to-wall alignment and integrated rainwater detailing can be part of the architectural brief. Price those requirements explicitly. Neither example has a published roof-only bill suitable for extracting a national per-m² rate.

sections.title: What should be itemised before comparing quotes?

items: Exact profile/variant, pan width, base metal, coating and thickness.
Seaming/clip system and required support or substrate.
Underlay and any separating or ventilation layers in the specified build-up.
Valleys, penetrations, transitions and integrated gutters.
Fabrication, curved work, transport and lifting where required.
Installer scope, maintenance documents and warranty responsibilities.

blocks.text: A visually simple wide pan can still be part of a detailed assembly. Ask for the cost difference in the actual specification, rather than an unexplained “premium roof” percentage.

sections.title: How do you compare with corrugate or five-rib?

blocks.text: Keep the same roof geometry and environmental requirements in the comparison, then allow the support and accessory scope to change where the chosen system requires it. A cheap pan that needs more associated work may not produce the cheapest completed assembly.
Minimum pitch is only one design constraint. This guide and the estimator do not certify a system for a roof. Use the current manufacturer details and the responsible designer’s assessment.

roof-pitch.title: How do you calculate roof pitch and its effect on area?
roof-pitch.description: Calculate NZ roof pitch from rise and run, convert plan area to sloping roof area and understand product-specific pitch limits without climbing onto a roof.
roof-pitch.answer: Roof pitch is the slope of a roof plane, usually expressed in degrees. From drawings, pitch = arctan(vertical rise ÷ horizontal run). To convert that plane’s horizontal projected area to its sloping area, divide by cos(pitch). Do not apply the conversion again to an actual sloping measurement.

sections.title: How do you find pitch from rise and run?

blocks.text: Rise is the vertical change; run is the horizontal distance over that same change. Use matching units. On a simple symmetrical gable, the run to the ridge is half the wall-to-wall span, before considering the particular dimension you are measuring. Do not confuse full span with run.

Worked example: a rise of 1.5 m over a horizontal run of 3 m gives arctan(1.5 ÷ 3) = 26.57°. The sloping length over that run is √(3² + 1.5²) = 3.354 m. These are geometry calculations, not structural design advice.

sections.title: How much does pitch add to roof area?

blocks.caption: Calculated surface area for a 150m² horizontal roof projection

blocks.text: The table assumes every part of the projected roof has the stated pitch and that eaves are already included. A flat result at 0° is a mathematical example, not permission to install the profiles discussed here on a flat roof.

sections.title: What pitch does the roof covering require?

blocks.caption: Examples, not a universal design schedule

cells: Minimum can increase with sheet length.

blocks.text: Do not choose a roof from the minimum-pitch column alone. The designer or supplier must confirm the complete specification. Existing sag, local low spots and junctions are not assessed by this calculator.

sections.title: Do all lineal measurements use the same multiplier?

blocks.text: No. A line that follows the roof’s steepest slope uses the rafter factor, while a level ridge normally does not change. Hips and valleys depend on their direction and the intersecting roof planes. Applying the area multiplier blindly to every line is wrong.

For the special case of equal-pitch planes meeting at a 45° plan diagonal, the hip or valley multiplier from its plan length is √(1 + tan²(pitch) ÷ 2). That simplification is not valid for arbitrary intersections or unequal pitches. Use measured three-dimensional geometry or appropriate design calculations for those cases.

sections.title: How can you obtain useful measurements safely?

blocks.text: Use architectural drawings, existing measured information or a competent survey. An aerial image normally supplies plan-view geometry, not reliable pitch by itself. Do not climb onto a roof to use a consumer angle app.

Calibrate a plan or image using a known dimension.
Check that the image is not perspective-distorted.
Separate roof planes with different pitches.
Keep unknown pitch visible instead of silently treating it as zero.

roof-area.title: How do you calculate the area of a roof?
roof-area.description: Calculate roof area from plans or actual measurements, understand eaves and pitch, and keep roof covering, material waste, removal and scaffold quantities separate.
roof-area.answer: Calculate each roof plane’s area, convert projected areas for pitch where needed, then add the planes. Keep eaves within the roof outline, and add material-order allowances separately. A house’s total floor area is not automatically its roof area, especially on a two-storey building.

sections.title: Which area have you been given?

blocks.caption: Area types used in a roofing estimate

cells: Internal or gross floor area, possibly across multiple storeys.
Starting context only; establish the roof outline.
Horizontal projection of the roof outline.
Area measured along the sloping planes.
Material quantity after layout, laps and cutting allowance.
Use for supply quantities, not automatically for removal.

blocks.text: If a listing says a house is 200m², ask what that figure includes. Halving a two-storey floor area is only a rough guess where floors overlap exactly. Garages, lower roofs, decks and offsets can make it misleading.

sections.title: Convert a roof projection to sloping area

blocks.text: The calculator assumes one pitch, or multiple planes all at the same pitch. For mixed pitches, calculate each plane separately and sum the results. If a plan area is 150m² at 25°, the sloping area is 165.5m², before any material-order allowance.

sections.title: How do eaves and overhangs affect the result?

blocks.text: Use the roof outline rather than just the outside walls. For a simple 10 m × 15 m rectangular building with a uniform 0.45 m horizontal overhang on all sides, the projected roof rectangle is 10.9 m × 15.9 m = 173.31m². At a uniform 25° pitch, that is about 191.2m² of sloping area.
This example is deliberately a simple geometry. Do not use its percentage uplift for another building. Gables, different overhangs, porches and intersecting roofs need their own dimensions.

sections.title: Which other measurements do you need?

blocks.caption: Area alone does not describe the entire roof

cells: Keep the relevant coverage/lap allowance explicit.
Record each type and whether measurements are plan or actual.
Record size and detail requirements separately.
Perimeter or scaffold area, depending on quote

blocks.text: A rectangle and a heavily cut-up roof can share the same area but have different edge lengths. This is why the detailed estimator asks for those components rather than inventing them from m² alone.

sections.title: Should you add wastage before calculating everything?

blocks.text: No. Keep net roof geometry and material ordering quantities separate. Cutting allowances belong to the relevant product layout; removal normally relates to the actual existing area removed. Adding the new sheet’s waste percentage to disposal or scaffold quantities is not justified.

For long-run sheets, effective cover and cut lengths control ordering. For tiles, panel coverage and the manufacturer’s layout matter. Do not use one universal percentage as a substitute for a measured takeoff.

sections.title: Can a satellite image or plan give an accurate result?

blocks.text: A calibrated drawing can give useful quantities. Accuracy still depends on scale, resolution, distortion, roof-outline visibility and correct pitch inputs. An oblique satellite image is not a flat plan merely because it looks clear. Confirm a known dimension and inspect the geometry before trusting the result.

items: Use a scale or known distance, not an assumed paper size.
Check at least a second dimension where possible.
Trace roof outlines rather than external walls.
Separate planes and pitches.
Review the quantities before applying a product rate.
Have ordering quantities verified before purchase.

faqs.q: Is roof area the same as floor area?
faqs.a: No. Floor area can include multiple storeys and need not include the roof overhangs. Establish the roof projection and pitch or use measured sloping roof planes.

faqs.q: Do I add pitch to measured sloping lengths?
faqs.a: No. Apply a plan-to-slope conversion only to projected measurements. The same geometry must not be converted twice.

scaffolding.title: What does roof scaffolding cost in New Zealand?
scaffolding.description: Compare scaffold price units, edge protection, setup and weekly hire with NZ supplier examples, clear scope limits and roof-access planning questions.
scaffolding.answer: Roof access prices depend on the system, height, perimeter, ground, working platforms and hire period. There is no single comparable “per-metre scaffold” price without those details. Full working scaffold and edge protection are different scopes, and scaffold elevation area is not roof area.

sections.title: What do NZ providers publish?

blocks.text: ScaffoldMe also reports a builder’s rental example: $4,000 setup/dismantle plus $190 per week, in the context of a 65 lm single-level package. The GST basis of that rental example is not explicit. It is not a current four-plank hire quotation.

We do not convert a three-plank supplier example into a verified four-plank rate. Upwell’s layout totals also differ from its headline rates and some example arithmetic is inconsistent. Confirm the actual quote; RoofHub does not copy those totals into the estimator.

sections.title: Is “per metre” length or area?

blocks.text: A lineal rate uses the measured run around the building. An elevation-area rate typically uses length × scaffold height, summed for the relevant faces. A roof-area rate is a third unit and cannot be substituted. Upwell explicitly describes the elevation-area approach.

For illustration only, a 60 m run at an assumed 3 m scaffold height is 180m² of elevation. At $18.50/m² setup and $1.50/m²/week, the arithmetic is $3,330 setup plus $270/week, excluding GST. It is not a four-plank quote, a design, or permission to assume that every single-storey building needs a 3 m scaffold.
That is also why simply multiplying a roof’s 200m² by a scaffolder’s m² rate can produce a wrong answer even though both numbers appear to use square metres.

sections.title: Can edge protection be used for a reroof?

blocks.text: Edge protection is a recognised risk-control approach, but it is not equivalent to a full working platform and it does not by itself address every roof-work hazard. A competent assessment must select suitable protection for the work and site.

RoofHub only offers the edge-protection planning option for eligible single-storey inputs. That is a product limitation, not a statement that NZ law bans it at two storeys. Selecting or excluding a cost estimate never waives the need for safe access.
WorkSafe’s older roof-work guide carries a notice about outdated legislation. We link it for the distinction between roof-edge and through-roof risks, not as a current compliance certificate.

sections.title: What does the RoofHub calculator assume?

blocks.text: Its working scaffold card separates one- and two-storey options, flat and difficult sites, and additional hire after four included weeks. Those ranges are project-planning allowances developed for this tool. They have not been converted into independently verified national tariffs.

A hillside can change the height, component quantities and work required. It may affect hire as well as setup, so the estimator’s simple rate should not be treated as a final sloping-site quote. Three-storey and unusual access remain site-specific.

sections.title: How long will the access be needed?

blocks.text: Coordinate the hire period with all trades. Roofing may finish before painting, cladding or window work. Confirm the starting event for rental, any minimum hire and the dismantling notice period.

sections.title: What should you request from a scaffolder?

items: A marked-up coverage plan and working heights.
Platform width and intended users/trades.
Edge protection, gates, stairs and loading requirements included.
Flat, sloping or restricted-access assumptions.
Delivery, erection, inspection, alteration and dismantling scope.
Included hire, extra weekly rate, GST and any permissions or engineering exclusions.

faqs.q: Is the estimator’s four-week hire period an industry rule?
faqs.a: No. It is the tool’s planning assumption. A scaffolder’s actual quote may use a different included or minimum period.
